strengths: The paper addresses an important gap: user-level private federated learning for large ASR models. Speaker-partitioned Common Voice data and adaptation from LibriSpeech seed models provide a useful benchmark incorporating heterogeneity and domain shift.

The measured benefits of per-layer clipping are substantial. At the same simulated noise level, Table 1 reduces English test WER from 31.1% with global clipping to 20.4% with dimension-based per-layer clipping. Gradient diagnostics and selective noise ablations provide useful evidence about optimization bottlenecks.

The empirical study is extensive, covering three languages, initialization, cohort size, data heterogeneity, optimizers, and models ranging from approximately 114M to 510M parameters. Transferring training settings across languages strengthens the practical value of the recipe.

Detailed preprocessing, training configurations, compute requirements, and a public code link support reproducibility. The manuscript explicitly identifies extrapolated results, nonprivate seed data, and diagnostic experiments without privacy guarantees. Its discussion of limitations and secure aggregation is constructive; no material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The central convergence claim is not established. Corollary 1 requires κ = 1 − 8(1 − η_loc T_loc)^2 > 0, but its prescribed η_loc = Θ(1/(L√(T_loc T))) makes κ approach −7 for fixed T_loc as T increases. Thus the displayed inequality becomes vacuous in the claimed asymptotic regime. The nonvanishing DP-noise term also prevents the bound from establishing convergence to a stationary point at fixed nonzero noise. These issues undermine the claimed convergence rate and recovery of prior guarantees.

The proof contains additional substantive gaps. Equations E.32–E.33 treat the adaptive preconditioner p^(t) as independent of the current DP noise, although Equations E.8–E.9 compute it from the same noisy update. The expectation factorization and subsequent cancellation therefore require correction. Equation E.19 also invokes uniformly bounded gradients, which do not follow from the stated smoothness and variance assumptions alone.

The headline privacy–utility results remain conditional projections. The corresponding measured English runs use 34,753 users and cohorts of 1,024, with reported ε values around 10^7–10^8. Obtaining ε = 4.5 or 7.2 requires extrapolation to approximately 7M or 70M users and cohorts near 205,000 while assuming comparable WER. This assumption is honestly disclosed, but population growth changes data diversity, participation, and optimization variance. The nonprivate cohort-scaling experiments do not sufficiently validate the projected private training behavior or deployment practicality.

The experiments do not isolate the claimed synergy between LAMB and per-layer clipping under DP. Tables 8–9 compare optimizers without DP, whereas the noisy clipping comparisons use LAMB throughout. Matched comparisons crossing optimizer and clipping choices at the same privacy/noise settings are needed to establish why this particular combination is essential and how it improves on existing adaptive optimization and clipping approaches.

Some conclusions overstate the evidence. Appendix H.7 claims consistent superiority across model sizes, but Table 21 reports worse WER for the deepest model with per-layer clipping: 26.4% versus 25.7%. Gains for French and German are also small, and repeated-run uncertainty is not reported. Additionally, the headline 1.3/4.6-point degradation uses the 19.1% nonprivate FL baseline; the corresponding gaps to the 17.8% centralized baseline are 2.6/5.9 points. These boundaries and comparison baselines should be explicit.
